prompt: Which tool estimates the cost of Azure services before you deploy them?

options.text: Cost analysis in Microsoft Cost Management

explanation: The pricing calculator builds estimates from planned products, sizes and regions.

why_wrong.a: Cost analysis shows costs already incurred.
why_wrong.c: Service Health reports on service issues.

prompt: Which data transfer is generally charged in Azure?

options.text: All data transfer is always free
Data leaving Azure datacenters to the internet
Data inside a single virtual machine
Data coming into Azure from the internet

explanation: Outbound data transfer is generally charged, while inbound is generally free.

why_wrong.c: Data within a VM is not network transfer.

prompt: Why might the same virtual machine cost a different amount in two regions?

options.text: Only the number of subscriptions affects price

why_wrong.b: Prices are not identical across regions.
why_wrong.a: Region affects price as well as latency.
why_wrong.d: Many factors, not only subscriptions, affect price.

prompt: Finance wants an alert when spending reaches 80% of a monthly limit. What should be created?

options.text: A budget with alerts in Microsoft Cost Management

explanation: Budgets can notify you when spending crosses a threshold.

prompt: What does cost analysis help you do?

options.text: Estimate costs of resources you have not created
See and break down where your costs come from over time

explanation: Cost analysis breaks down actual spending by resource, group, tag or period.

why_wrong.a: Naming rules are enforced with governance tools.
why_wrong.b: Cost analysis does not create resources.

prompt: What is a tag in Azure?

options.text: A name and value pair attached to a resource to help organise it

explanation: Tags are labels such as Department = Finance.

why_wrong.c: Permissions are granted through role assignments.

prompt: A company wants to report Azure costs by department. What should it use?

options.text: Tags such as a Department tag, then group costs by tag

explanation: Tags let you group and filter costs by department, project or environment.

why_wrong.b: Availability sets group VMs for resilience.

prompt: By default, do resources automatically inherit the tags applied to their resource group?

options.text: No, unless you set it up, for example with Azure Policy

explanation: Tags are not inherited by default.

why_wrong.d: No resource type inherits by default.
why_wrong.b: No resource type inherits by default.

prompt: Which option lets an organisation reuse eligible existing Windows Server licences on Azure to reduce cost?
explanation: Azure Hybrid Benefit lets you apply eligible existing licences to Azure.

prompt: Which TWO factors can affect Azure costs? (Select two.)

options.text: The browser you use for the portal

explanation: Resource type, size and region are cost factors.

why_wrong.e: The browser does not change cost.
why_wrong.a: The theme does not change cost.
why_wrong.d: The keyboard does not change cost.

prompt: Which TWO describe the Azure pricing calculator? (Select two.)

options.text: It lets you compare options by changing size, region and settings
It estimates the cost of planned Azure resources
It stops resources automatically when a budget is reached

explanation: The calculator is a planning tool that produces estimates for different configurations.

why_wrong.a: Invoices come from billing, not the calculator.
why_wrong.e: Budgets alert; they do not stop resources.
why_wrong.b: Tags are applied to resources, not by the calculator.

prompt: Decide whether each statement is true.

options.text: Budgets in Cost Management can send alerts when spending reaches a threshold.
A budget automatically shuts down resources by itself.
Tags can help group costs by project or department.

explanation: Budgets alert and tags help group costs, but budgets do not stop resources on their own.

why_wrong.s1: Yes. Alerts are a main feature.
why_wrong.s2: No. A budget does not stop resources by itself.
why_wrong.s3: Yes. Cost analysis can group by tag.

prompt: Which option gives a discount for committing to specific capacity for one or three years and suits steady, predictable workloads?
explanation: Reservations trade a one- or three-year commitment for discounted pricing.

why_wrong.d: Spot uses unused capacity and can be interrupted.
why_wrong.c: Pay-as-you-go has no commitment and no discount.
why_wrong.a: Tags are labels, not a pricing option.

prompt: What do you commit to with an Azure savings plan for compute?

options.text: A monthly amount of outbound data
A specific VM family and size
An hourly spend amount for one or three years

explanation: A savings plan commits you to spend, not to a particular VM type.

why_wrong.a: Data transfer is not what a savings plan covers.

prompt: Batch rendering jobs can restart if interrupted, and the team wants the lowest possible price. What fits best?
explanation: Spot suits interruptible, fault-tolerant work at the lowest price.

why_wrong.c: A savings plan suits steady usage that needs flexibility.
why_wrong.b: Hybrid Benefit applies existing licences; it is not a way to use spare capacity.

prompt: Decide whether each statement is true.

options.text: Spot virtual machines can be interrupted when Azure needs the capacity back.
Reservations are best for unpredictable, short-lived workloads.
A savings plan for compute lets you commit to spending rather than to a specific VM type.

explanation: Spot can be interrupted, reservations suit stable workloads, and a savings plan commits to spend.

why_wrong.s1: Yes. That is the trade-off for the lower price.
why_wrong.s2: No. Reservations suit steady, predictable workloads.
why_wrong.s3: Yes. That is the main difference from a reservation.
